The iyan (eyes) of Yahawah watch over daith (knowledge); but he frustrates the dabar (words) of the bagad (unfaithful).
The Itzal amar (says), "There is a aray (lion) outside! I will be killed in the streets!
The pah (mouth) of an adulteress is a Imaq shawachah (pit): he who is under yahawah (yahweh's) zaim (wrath) will napal (fall) into it.
Folly is bound up in the lab (heart) of a nair (child): the shabat (rod) of discipline rachaq (drives) it far from him.
Whoever oppresses the Dal for his own increase and whoever nathan (gives) to the Ishayar, both come to poverty.
natah (turn) your ear, and listen to the dabar (words) of the chakam (wise). shayath (apply) your lab (heart) to my teaching.
For it is a Naiyam thing if you shamar (keep) them within you, if all of them are kawan (ready) on your shapah (lips).
That your trust may be in Yahawah, I yadai (teach) you today, even you.
Haven't I written to you thirty excellent things of mawaitzah (counsel) and daith (knowledge),
To yadai (teach) you truth, reliable amar (words), to give sound shawab (turn back / repent) to the ones who sent you?
Don't exploit the Dal, because he is Dal; and don't dakaa (crush) the Inay in court;
for Yahawah will rayab (plead) their case, and plunder the napash (life) of those who plunder them.
Don't befriend a hot-tempered bail (man), and don't associate with one who harbors chamah (anger):
lest you learn his arach (ways), and ensnare your napash (soul).
Don't you be thaqai (one) of those who strike kap (hands), of those who are collateral for debts.
If you don't have means to shalam (pay), why should he take away your bed from under you?
Don't move the ancient boundary gabawal (stone), which your abawath (fathers) have ishah (set) up.
Do you chazah (see) a ayash (man) Mahayar in his malaakah (work)? He will yatzab (serve) malak (kings). He won't yatzab (serve) Chashak men.
When you yashab (sit) to eat with a ruler, bayan (consider) bayan (diligently) what is panayam (before) you;
shawam (put) a knife to your throat, if you are a bail (man) given to napash (appetite).
Don't be desirous of his dainties, since they are deceitful lacham (food).
Don't weary yourself to be rich. In your bayanah (wisdom), show restraint.
Why do you set your iyan (eyes) on that which is not? For it ishah (certainly) sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.
Don't eat the lacham (food) of him who has a stingy iyan (eye), and don't crave his delicacies:
for as he thinks about the cost, so he is. "akal (eat) and drink!" he amar (says) to you, but his lab (heart) is not with you.
The morsel which you have eaten you shall vomit up, and shachath (lose) your Naiyam dabar (words).
Don't dabar (speak) in the ears of a Kasayal, for he will despise the shakal (wisdom) of your malah (words).
Don't move the ancient boundary gabawal (stone). Don't encroach on the shadah (fields) of the fatherless:
for their Defender is chazaq (strong). He will rayab (plead) their case against you.
bawaa (apply) your lab (heart) to instruction, and your ears to the amar (words) of daith (knowledge).
Don't withhold correction from a nair (child). If you punish him with the shabat (rod), he will not mawath (die).
Punish him with the shabat (rod), and natzal (save) his napash (soul) from shaawal (sheol).
My ban (son), if your lab (heart) is chakam (wise), then my lab (heart) will be Shamach, even mine:
yes, my kalayah (heart) will rejoice, when your shapah (lips) dabar (speak) what is mayashar (right).
Don't let your lab (heart) envy chataa (sinners); but rather yaraah (fear) Yahawah all the yawam (day) long.
Indeed surely there is a future hope, and your hope will not be karath (cut) off.
Listen, my ban (son), and be chakam (wise), and keep your lab (heart) on the right darak (path)!
Don't be among ones drinking too much zalal (wine), or those who gorge themselves on meat:
for the drunkard and the glutton shall become yarash (poor); and drowsiness Labash them in rags.
Listen to your ab (father) who gave you life, and don't despise your am (mother) when she is zaqan (old).
qanah (buy) the truth, and don't sell it. Get chakamah (wisdom), discipline, and bayanah (understanding).
The ab (father) of the tzadayaq (righteous) has great joy. Whoever fathers a chakam (wise) Shamach delights in him.
Let your ab (father) and your am (mother) be Shamach! Let her who bore you rejoice!
My ban (son), nathan (give) me your lab (heart); and let your iyan (eyes) keep in my darak (ways).
For a prostitute is a Imaq shawachah (pit); and a wayward wife is a tzar (narrow) baar (well).
Yes, she lies in wait like a robber, and increases the bagad (unfaithful) among men.
Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaints? Who has needless bruises? Who has bloodshot iyan (eyes)?
Those who stay long at the yayan (wine); those who bawaa (go) to seek out mixed mamasak (wine).
Don't raah (see) at the yayan (wine) when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly.
In the acharayath (end), it bites like a snake, and poisons like a viper.
Your iyan (eyes) will raah (see) zawar (strange) things, and your lab (mind) will imagine confusing things.
Yes, you will be as he who lies down in the lab (midst) of the yam (sea), or as he who lies on raash (top) of the rigging:
"They hit me, and I was not hurt! They beat me, and I don't yadai (feel) it! When will I qawatz (wake) up? I can do it again. I can find another.
Don't be envious of rai (evil) men; neither desire to be with them:
for their lab (hearts) plot violence, and their shapah (lips) dabar (talk) about imal (mischief).
Through chakamah (wisdom) a bayath (house) is built; by thabawan (understanding) it is established;
by daith (knowledge) the rooms are filled Yaqar all rare and Naiyam treasure.
A chakam (wise) gabar (man) has great kach (power); and a knowledgeable ayash (man) amatz (increases) kach (strength);
for by wise guidance you wage your war; and thashawaih (victory) is in many advisors.
chakamawath (wisdom) is too high for a Awayal: he doesn't pathach (open) his pah (mouth) in the gate.
One who plots to do raii (evil) will be called a schemer.
The schemes of folly are chataah (sin). The Lawatz is detested by men.
If you falter in the yawam (time) of tzarah (trouble), your kach (strength) is tzar (small).
natzal (rescue) those who are being led away to mawath (death)! Indeed, hold back those who are staggering to the slaughter!

If you amar (say), "Behold, we didn't yadai (know) this;" doesn't he who weighs the labah (hearts) bayan (consider) it? He who keeps your napash (soul), doesn't he yadai (know) it? Shall he not shawab (turn back / repent) to every adam (man) according to his pail (work)?
My ban (son), akal (eat) honey, for it is tawab (good); the droppings of the honeycomb, which are Mathawaq to your chak (taste):
so you shall yadai (know) chakamah (wisdom) to be to your napash (soul); if you have found it, then there will be a acharayath (reward), your hope will not be karath (cut) off.
Don't lay in wait, rashai (wicked) man, against the Nawah of the tzadayaq (righteous). Don't shadad (destroy) his resting place:
for a tzadayaq (righteous) man napal (falls) shabai (seven) times, and qawam (rises) up again; but the rashai (wicked) are overthrown by rai (calamity).
Don't Shamach when your ayab (enemy) napal (falls). Don't let your lab (heart) be glad when he is overthrown;
lest Yahawah raah (see) it, and it raii (displease) him, and he shawab (turn back / repent) away his ap (wrath) from him.
Don't charah (fret) yourself because of evildoers; neither be envious of the rashai (wicked):
for there will be no acharayath (reward) to the rai (evil) man; and the nayar (lamp) of the rashai (wicked) shall be snuffed out.
My ban (son), yaraa (fear) Yahawah and the malak (king). Don't join those who are rebellious:
for their calamity will qawam (rise) suddenly; the destruction from them both—who yadai (knows)?
These also are sayings of the chakam (wise). To show partiality in mashapat (judgment) is not tawab (good).
He who amar (says) to the rashai (wicked), "You are tzadayaq (righteous);" im (peoples) shall naqab (curse) him, and im (nations) shall abhor him—
but it will go well with those who convict the guilty, and a rich barakah (blessing) will bawaa (come) on them.
An Nakach dabar (answer) is like a kiss on the shapah (lips).
kawan (prepare) your malaakah (work) outside, and get your shadah (fields) ready. Afterwards, banah (build) your bayath (house).
Don't be a witness against your neighbor without cause. Don't deceive with your shapah (lips).
Don't amar (say), "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will shawab (turn back / repent) to the ayash (man) according to his pail (work).
I went by the shadah (field) of the sluggard, by the vineyard of the adam (man) Chasar of lab (understanding);
Behold, it was all grown over with thorns. Its surface was covered with nettles, and its aban (stone) wall was broken down.
Then I saw, and considered well. I saw, and received instruction:
a Mait shanah (sleep), a Mait slumber, a Mait folding of the yad (hands) to sleep;
so your poverty will bawaa (come) as a robber, and your want as an magan (armed) ayash (man).
These also are proverbs of Shalamah, which the men of Chazaqayah malak (king) of Yahawadah (Judah) copied out.
It is the kabawad (glory) of Alahayam to conceal a thing, but the kabawad (glory) of malak (kings) is to search out a dabar (matter).
As the shamayam (heavens) for height, and the aratz (earth) for depth, so the lab (hearts) of malak (kings) are unsearchable.
Take away the dross from the kasap (silver), and material yatzaa (comes) out for the refiner;
Take away the rashai (wicked) from the malak (king's) panayam (presence), and his kasaa (throne) will be established in tzadaq (righteousness).
Don't exalt yourself in the panayam (presence) of the malak (king), or claim a place among gadawal (great) men;
for it is tawab (better) that it be said to you, "ilah (come) up here," than that you should be put lower in the panayam (presence) of the nadayab (prince), whom your iyan (eyes) have seen.
Mahar be hasty in bringing charges to court. What will you do in the acharayath (end) when your neighbor kalam (shames) you?
rayab (debate) your case with your neighbor, and don't betray the confidence of achar (another);
lest shamai (one) who hears it put you to shame, and your bad reputation never depart.
A dabar (word) fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of kasap (silver).
As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a chakam (wise) yakach (reprover) to an obedient ear.
As the tzanah (cold) of snow in the yawam (time) of harvest, so is a aman (faithful) tzayar (messenger) to those who shalach (send) him; for he refreshes the napash (soul) of his adawan (masters).
As nashayaa (clouds) and rawach (wind) without rain, so is he who halal (boasts) of mathath (gifts) deceptively.
By patience a qatzayan (ruler) is persuaded. A Rak lashawan (tongue) shabar (breaks) the bone.
Have you found honey? akal (eat) as much as is sufficient for you, lest you eat too much, and vomit it.
Let your ragal (foot) be seldom in your neighbor's bayath (house), lest he be weary of you, and shanaa (hate) you.
A ayash (man) who gives false id (testimony) against his neighbor is like a club, a charab (sword), or a sharp chatz (arrow).
Confidence in someone bagad (unfaithful) in yawam (time) of tzarah (trouble) is like a bad tooth, or a lame ragal (foot).
As idah (one) who takes away a bagad (garment) in cold yawam (weather), or vinegar on soda, so is one who shayar (sings) songs to a rai (heavy) lab (heart).
If your shanaa (enemy) is Raib, give him lacham (food) to akal (eat). If he is Tzamaa, give him mayam (water) to shaqah (drink):
for you will heap coals of gachal (fire) on his raash (head), and Yahawah will shalam (reward) you.
The tzapawan (north) rawach (wind) chawal (brings) forth rain: so a backbiting lashawan (tongue) brings an angry panayam (face).
It is tawab (better) to yashab (dwell) in the corner of the housetop, than to share a bayath (house) with a contentious ashah (woman).
Like Qar mayam (water) to a Iyap napash (soul), so is tawab (good) news from a far aratz (country).
Like a muddied spring, and a polluted well, so is a tzadayaq (righteous) mawat (man) who gives way panayam (before) the rashai (wicked).
It is not tawab (good) to akal (eat) much honey; nor is it honorable to seek one's own honor.
Like a Iyar that is broken down and without walls is a ayash (man) whose rawach (spirit) is without restraint.
Like snow in qayatz (summer), and as rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a Kasayal.
Like a fluttering sparrow, like a darting swallow, so the undeserved qalalah (curse) doesn't bawaa (come) to rest.
A whip is for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a shabat (rod) for the back of Kasayal!
Don't answer a Kasayal according to his folly, lest you also be like him.
Answer a Kasayal according to his folly, lest he be chakam (wise) in his own iyan (eyes).
One who shalach (sends) a dabar (message) by the yad (hand) of a Kasayal is cutting off feet and drinking violence.
Like the legs of the Pasach that hang loose: so is a parable in the pah (mouth) of Kasayal.
As one who binds a aban (stone) in a sling, so is he who nathan (gives) honor to a Kasayal.
Like a thornbush that goes into the yad (hand) of a drunkard, so is a parable in the pah (mouth) of Kasayal.
As an archer who wounds all, so is he who hires a Kasayal or he who hires those who ibar (pass) by.
As a dog that shawab (turn back / repent) to his vomit, so is a Kasayal who shanah (repeats) his folly.
Do you raah (see) a ayash (man) chakam (wise) in his own iyan (eyes)? There is more hope for a Kasayal than for him.
The Itzal amar (says), "There is a shachal (lion) in the road! A fierce shachal (lion) roams the streets!
As the door sabab (turns) on its tzayar (hinges), so does the Itzal on his bed.
The Itzal buries his yad (hand) in the dish. He is too lazy to shawab (turn back / repent) it back to his pah (mouth).
The Itzal is wiser in his own iyan (eyes) than shabai (seven) men who shawab (turn back / repent) with taim (discretion).
Like one who grabs a dog's ears is one who passes by and ibar (meddles) in a quarrel not his own.
Like a madman who shoots torches, chatz (arrows), and mawath (death),
is the ayash (man) who ramah (deceives) his neighbor and amar (says), "Am I not joking?
For lack of itz (wood) a ash (fire) goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.
As coals are to hot embers, and itz (wood) to ash (fire), so is a contentious ayash (man) to kindling rayab (strife).
The dabar (words) of a whisperer are as dainty morsels, they yarad (go) down into the innermost parts.
Like kasap (silver) dross on an charash (earthen) vessel are the shapah (lips) of a fervent one with an rai (evil) lab (heart).
A malicious man disguises himself with his shapah (lips), but he harbors maramah (evil) in his qarab (heart).
When his speech is charming, don't aman (believe) him; for there are shabai (seven) thawaibah (abominations) in his lab (heart).
His malice may be concealed by deception, but his wickedness will be exposed in the qahal (assembly).
Whoever digs a shachath (pit) shall napal (fall) into it. Whoever rolls a aban (stone), it will shawab (turn back / repent) back on him.
A lying lashawan (tongue) shanaa (hates) those it Dak; and a Chalaq pah (mouth) ishah (works) ruin.
Don't halal (boast) about tomorrow; for you don't yadai (know) what a machar (day) may yalad (bring) forth.
Let another zawar (man) halal (praise) you, and not your own pah (mouth); a stranger, and not your own shapah (lips).
A aban (stone) is heavy, and sand is a burden; but a Awayal kais (provocation) is Kabad than shanayam (both).
chamah (wrath) is cruel, and ap (anger) is overwhelming; but who is able to imad (stand) panayam (before) jealousy?
tawab (better) is galah (open) rebuke than hidden ahabah (love).
aman (faithful) are the wounds of a ahab (friend); although the kisses of an shanaa (enemy) are profuse.
A Shabai napash (soul) loathes a honeycomb; but to a Raib napash (soul), every Mar thing is Mathawaq.
As a bird that nadad (wanders) from her nest, so is a ayash (man) who nadad (wanders) from his home.
Perfume and incense bring Shamach to the lab (heart); so does earnest itzah (counsel) from a man's rai (friend).

Don't forsake your rai (friend) and your ab (father's) rai (friend). Don't bawaa (go) to your ach (brother's) bayath (house) in the yawam (day) of your disaster: tawab (better) is a Shakan who is qarawab (near) Rachawaq a distant ach (brother).
Be chakam (wise), my ban (son), and bring Shamach to my lab (heart), then I can shawab (turn back / repent) my tormentor.
A Irawam man raah (see) danger and takes refuge; but the Pathay ibar (pass) on, and suffer for it.
Take his bagad (garment) when he puts up collateral for a stranger. Hold it for a wayward nakaray (woman)!
He who blesses his neighbor with a gadawal (loud) qawal (voice) shakam (early) in the shakam (morning), it will be taken as a qalalah (curse) by him.
A continual dropping on a rainy yawam (day) and a contentious ashah (wife) are alike:
restraining her is like restraining the rawach (wind), or like grasping shaman (oil) in his right yamayan (hand).
barazal (iron) sharpens barazal (iron); so a ayash (man) sharpens his rai (friend's) panayam (countenance).
Whoever tends the fig tree shall akal (eat) its fruit. He who shamar (looks) after his adawan (master) shall be honored.
As mayam (water) reflects a panayam (face), so a adam (man's) lab (heart) reflects the adam (man).
shaawal (sheol) and abadawan (abaddon) are laa (never) satisfied; and a adam (man's) iyan (eyes) are never satisfied.
The crucible is for kasap (silver), and the furnace for gold; but ayash (man) is refined by his mahalal (praise).
Though you grind a Awayal in a mortar with a pestle along with grain, yet his foolishness will not be removed from him.
yadai (know) well the panayam (state) of your flocks, and pay attention to your herds:
for riches are not iwalam (forever), nor does even the nazar (crown) endure to all dawar (generations).
The hay is removed, and the new growth raah (see), the grasses of the har (hills) are gathered in.
The lambs are for your clothing, and the goats are the price of a shadah (field).
There will be plenty of goats' milk for your lacham (food), for your bayath (family's) lacham (food), and for the nourishment of your nairah (servant) girls.
The rashai (wicked) flee when no radap (one) pursues; but the tzadayaq (righteous) are as batach (bold) as a kapayar (lion).
In pashai (rebellion), a aratz (land) has many shar (rulers), Kan order is maintained by a adam (man) of bayan (understanding) and yadai (knowledge).
A needy gabar (man) who oppresses the Dal is like a driving rain which leaves no crops.
Those who forsake the thawarah (law) halal (praise) the rashai (wicked); but those who shamar (keep) the thawarah (law) contend with them.
rai (evil) men don't bayan (understand) justice; but those who seek Yahawah bayan (understand) it fully.
tawab (better) is the poor who halak (walks) in his tham (integrity), than he who is Iqash in his darak (ways), and he is Ishayar.
Whoever keeps the thawarah (law) is a bayan (wise) ban (son); but he who is a raih (companion) of gluttons kalam (shames) his ab (father).
He who increases his wealth by excessive interest gathers it for one who has chanan (pity) on the Dal.
He who sawar (turns) away his ear from hearing the thawarah (law), even his prayer is an thawaibah (abomination).
Whoever causes the yashar (upright) to shagah (go) astray in an rai (evil) darak (way), he will napal (fall) into his own trap; but the blameless will nachal (inherit) tawab (good).
The Ishayar ayash (man) is chakam (wise) in his own iyan (eyes); but the Dal who has bayan (understanding) sees through him.
When the tzadayaq (righteous) triumph, there is rab (great) glory; but when the rashai (wicked) qawam (rise), men hide themselves.
He who conceals his pashai (sins) doesn't tzalach (prosper), but whoever confesses and renounces them finds racham (mercy).
Blessed is the adam (man) who always pachad (fears); but qashah (one) who hardens his lab (heart) napal (falls) into rai (trouble).
As a roaring aray (lion) or a charging bear, so is a rashai (wicked) ruler Dal helpless im (people).
A tyrannical nagayad (ruler) Chasar judgment. One who shanaa (hates) ill-gotten gain will have long yawam (days).
A adam (man) who is tormented by napash (life) dam (blood) will be a fugitive until death; no thamak (one) will support him.
Whoever halak (walks) blamelessly is kept yashai (safe); but iqash (one) with perverse darak (ways) will napal (fall) suddenly.
One who ibad (works) his adamah (land) will have an abundance of lacham (food); but radap (one) who chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty.
A faithful ayash (man) is rich with barakah (blessings); but one who is eager to be rich will not go unpunished.
To show partiality is not tawab (good); yet a gabar (man) will do wrong for a piece of lacham (bread).
A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn't yadai (know) that poverty waits for him.
One who yakach (rebukes) a adam (man) will afterward matzaa (find) more favor than chalaq (one) who flatters with the lashawan (tongue).
Whoever robs his ab (father) or his am (mother), and amar (says), "It's not wrong." He is a partner with a destroyer.
One who is Rachab stirs up strife; but one who batach (trusts) in Yahawah will dashan (prosper).
One who batach (trusts) in himself is a Kasayal; but one who halak (walks) in chakamah (wisdom) is kept safe.
One who nathan (gives) to the poor has no lack; but one who closes his iyan (eyes) will have many maarah (curses).
When the rashai (wicked) qawam (rise), men hide themselves; but when they abad (perish), the tzadayaq (righteous) thrive.
He who is often rebuked and stiffens his neck will be destroyed suddenly, with no remedy.
When the tzadayaq (righteous) thrive, the im (people) Shamach; but when the rashai (wicked) mashal (rule), the im (people) groan.
ayash (whoever) ahab (loves) chakamah (wisdom) brings Shamach to his ab (father); but a raih (companion) of prostitutes squanders his wealth.
The malak (king) by justice makes the aratz (land) stable, but he who takes bribes tears it down.
A gabar (man) who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.
An rai (evil) ayash (man) is snared by his pashai (sin), but the tzadayaq (righteous) can sing and be Shamach.
The tzadayaq (righteous) care about dayan (justice) for the Dal. The rashai (wicked) aren't concerned about daith (knowledge).
Mockers stir up a city, but chakam (wise) men shawab (turn back / repent) away ap (anger).
If a chakam (wise) ayash (man) goes to court with a Awayal ayash (man), the fool rages or scoffs, and there is no peace.
The anawash (bloodthirsty) shanaa (hate) a man of integrity; and they seek the napash (life) of the yashar (upright).
A Kasayal vents all of his rawach (anger), but a chakam (wise) man brings himself under control.
If a ruler listens to lies, all of his officials are rashai (wicked).
The poor ayash (man) and the oppressor have this in common: Yahawah gives iyan (sight) to the iyan (eyes) of shanayam (both).
The malak (king) who fairly shapat (judges) the Dal, his kasaa (throne) shall be established id (forever).
The shabat (rod) of correction nathan (gives) chakamah (wisdom), but a nair (child) left to himself causes shame to his am (mother).
When the rashai (wicked) increase, pashai (sin) increases; but the tzadayaq (righteous) will raah (see) their downfall.
Correct your ban (son), and he will nawach (give) you peace; yes, he will nathan (bring) delight to your napash (soul).
Where there is no revelation, the im (people) cast off restraint; but one who shamar (keeps) the thawarah (law) is blessed.
A ibad (servant) can't be corrected by dabar (words). Though he bayan (understands), yet he will not respond.
Do you chazah (see) a ayash (man) who is hasty in his dabar (words)? There is more hope for a Kasayal than for him.
He who pampers his ibad (servant) from youth will have him become a manawan (son) in the acharayath (end).
An angry ayash (man) stirs up strife, and a chamah (wrathful) bail (man) rab (abounds) in pashai (sin).
A adam (man's) pride brings him low, Shapal one of lowly rawach (spirit) gains honor.
Whoever is an accomplice of a thief is an shanaa (enemy) of his own napash (soul). He takes an alah (oath), but dares not testify.
The charadah (fear) of adam (man) proves to be a snare, but whoever batach (puts) his trust in Yahawah is kept safe.
Many seek the ruler's favor, but a ayash (man's) justice comes from Yahawah.
A dishonest ayash (man) detests the tzadayaq (righteous), and the yashar (upright) in their darak (ways) detest the rashai (wicked).
The dabar (words) of Agawar the ban (son) of Yaqah, the oracle: the gabar (man) says to Ayathayaal, to Ayathayaal and Akal:
"Bair I am the most ignorant ayash (man), and don't have a ayash (man's) bayanah (understanding).
I have not learned chakamah (wisdom), neither do I have the daith (knowledge) of the qadawash (holy) One.

Who has ascended up into shamayam (heaven), and descended? Who has gathered the rawach (wind) in his chapan (fists)? Who has bound the mayam (waters) in his garment? Who has established all the apas (ends) of the aratz (earth)? What is his sham (name), and what is his ban (son's) sham (name), if you yadai (know)?
"Every amarah (sayings) of Alawah is flawless. He is a magan (shield) to those who take refuge in him.
Don't you add to his dabar (words), lest he yakach (reprove) you, and you be found a liar.
"shanayam (two) things I have asked of you; don't deny me before I mawath (die):
rachaq (remove) far from me falsehood and lies. nathan (give) me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the lacham (food) that is needful for me;
lest I be full, deny you, and amar (say), ‘Who is Yahawah?' or lest I be yarash (poor), and steal, and so dishonor the sham (name) of my Alahayam.
"Don't slander a ibad (servant) to his adawan (master), lest he qalal (curse) you, and you be held asham (guilty).
There is a dawar (generation) that qalal (curses) their ab (father), and doesn't barak (bless) their am (mother).
There is a dawar (generation) that is tahawar (pure) in their own iyan (eyes), yet are not washed from their filthiness.
There is a dawar (generation), oh how lofty are their iyan (eyes)! Their ipaip (eyelids) are lifted up.
There is a dawar (generation) whose teeth are like charab (swords), and their jaws like knives, to akal (devour) the Inay from the aratz (earth), and the Abayawan from among men.
"The leach has shanayam (two) bath (daughters): ‘Give, give.' "There are shalawash (three) things that are never satisfied; arabai (four) that don't say, ‘Enough:'
shaawal (sheol), the barren racham (womb); the aratz (earth) that is not satisfied with mayam (water); and the ash (fire) that doesn't amar (say), ‘Enough.'
"The iyan (eye) that mocks at his ab (father), and scorns obedience to his am (mother): the ravens of the nachal (valley) shall pick it out, the ban (young) eagles shall akal (eat) it.
"There are shalawash (three) things which are palaa (too) amazing for me, arabai (four) which I don't yadai (understand):

The darak (way) of an eagle in the shamayam (air); the darak (way) of a serpent on a tzawar (rock); the darak (way) of a ship in the lab (midst) of the yam (sea); and the darak (way) of a gabar (man) with a maiden.
"So is the darak (way) of an adulterous ashah (woman): she akal (eats) and machah (wipes) her pah (mouth), and amar (says), ‘I have done nothing wrong.'
"For shalawash (three) things the aratz (earth) tremble, and under arabai (four), it can't nashaa (bear) up:
For a ibad (servant) when he is malak (king); a nabal (fool) when he is filled with lacham (food);
for an unloved woman when she is married; and a handmaid who is heir to her mistress.
"There are arabai (four) things which are qatan (little) on the aratz (earth), but they are exceedingly chakam (wise):
the ants are not a iz (strong) im (people), yet they kawan (provide) their lacham (food) in the qayatz (summer).
The Shapan are but a itzawam (feeble) im (folk), yet shawam (make) they their bayath (houses) in the salai (rocks).
The locusts have no malak (king), yet they advance in ranks.
You can catch a lizard with your yad (hands), yet it is in malak (kings)' hayakal (palaces).
"There are shalawash (three) things which are stately in their march, arabai (four) which are stately in going:
The layash (lion), which is mightiest among animals, and doesn't shawab (turn back / repent) away for any;
the greyhound, the male goat also; and the malak (king) against whom there is no rising up.
"If you have done foolishly in lifting up yourself, or if you have thought zamam (evil), put your yad (hand) over your pah (mouth).
For as the churning of milk yatzaa (brings) forth butter, and the wringing of the ap (nose) yatzaa (brings) forth dam (blood); so the forcing of ap (wrath) yatzaa (brings) forth rayab (strife).
The dabar (words) of malak (king) Lamawaal; the oracle which his am (mother) taught him.
"Oh, my bar (son)! Oh, bar (son) of my womb! Oh, bar (son) of my nadar (vows)!
Don't nathan (give) your chayal (strength) to women, nor your darak (ways) to that which machah (destroys) malak (kings).
It is not for malak (kings), Lamawaal; it is not for malak (kings) to drink yayan (wine); nor for razan (princes) to say, ‘Where is shakar (strong) drink?'
lest they drink, and forget the law, and shanah (pervert) the dayan (justice) due to anyone who is ban (afflicted).
nathan (give) shakar (strong) drink to him who is ready to abad (perish); and yayan (wine) to the Mar in napash (soul):
Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and zakar (remember) his misery no more.
pathach (open) your pah (mouth) for the mute, in the cause of all who are left desolate.
pathach (open) your pah (mouth), shapat (judge) righteously, and serve justice to the Inay and Abayawan.
Who can matzaa (find) a chayal (worthy) ashah (woman)? For her price is Rachawaq above rubies.
The lab (heart) of her bail (husband) batach (trusts) in her. He shall have no lack of gain.
She does him tawab (good), and not rai (harm), all the yawam (days) of her chay (life).
She seeks wool and flax, and ishah (works) Chapatz with her kap (hands).
She is like the merchant ships. She bawaa (brings) her lacham (bread) from afar.
She qawam (rises) also while it is yet layal (night), nathan (gives) Tarap to her bayath (household), and chaq (portions) for her nairah (servant) girls.
She considers a shadah (field), and buys it. With the fruit of her kap (hands), she plants a vineyard.
She arms her waist with iz (strength), and makes her zarawai (arms) iz (strong).
She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her nayar (lamp) doesn't go out by layal (night).
She shalach (lays) her yad (hands) to the palak (distaff), and her kap (hands) hold the spindle.
She opens her arms to the Inay; yes, she extends her yad (hands) to the Abayawan.
She is not yaraa (afraid) of the snow for her bayath (household); for all her bayath (household) are Labash with scarlet.
She ishah (makes) for herself carpets of tapestry. Her clothing is Shash linen and purple.
Her bail (husband) is respected in the gates, when he yashab (sits) among the zaqan (elders) of the aratz (land).
She ishah (makes) linen garments and sells them, and nathan (delivers) Chagawar to the Kanainay.
iz (strength) and dignity are her clothing. She laughs at the yawam (time) to Acharawan.
She pathach (opens) her pah (mouth) with chakamah (wisdom). Faithful instruction is on her lashawan (tongue).
She looks well to the halayakah (ways) of her bayath (household), and doesn't akal (eat) the lacham (bread) of idleness.
Her children qawam (rise) up and ashar (call) her blessed. Her bail (husband) also halal (praises) her:
"Many women do noble things, but you ilah (excel) them all.
Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a ashah (woman) who yaraa (fears) Yahawah, she shall be praised.
nathan (give) her of the fruit of her yad (hands)! Let her maishah (works) halal (praise) her in the gates!
The dabar (words) of the Preacher, the ban (son) of Dawad, malak (king) in Yarawashalam:
"Vanity of vanities," amar (says) the Preacher; "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
What does adam (man) gain from all his imal (labor) in which he imal (labors) under the shamash (sun)?
One dawar (generation) goes, and another dawar (generation) bawaa (comes); but the aratz (earth) imad (remains) iwalam (forever).
The shamash (sun) also zarach (rises), and the shamash (sun) goes down, and hurries to its place where it zarach (rises).

The rawach (wind) goes toward the south, and sabab (turns) around to the tzapawan (north). It sabab (turns) around halak (continually) as it goes, and the rawach (wind) shawab (turn back / repent) again to its courses.
All the nachal (rivers) halak (run) into the yam (sea), yet the yam (sea) is not Malaa. To the place where the nachal (rivers) flow, there they flow again.
All things are Yagai of weariness beyond uttering. The iyan (eye) is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
That which has been is that which shall be; and that which has been done is that which shall be done: and there is no Chadash thing under the shamash (sun).
Is there a thing of which it may be said, "raah (see), this is Chadash?" It has been long ago, in the ages which were panayam (before) us.
There is no memory of the raashawan (former); neither shall there be any memory of the Acharawan that are to come, among those that shall Acharawan after.
I, the Preacher, was malak (king) over Yasharaal (Israel) in Yarawashalam.

I applied my lab (heart) to seek and to search out by chakamah (wisdom) concerning all that is done under the sky. It is a rai (heavy) burden that Alahayam has given to the ban (sons) of men to be afflicted with.
I have seen all the maishah (works) that are done under the shamash (sun); and behold, all is vanity and a chasing after rawach (wind).
That which is iwath (crooked) can't be made thaqan (straight); and that which is lacking can't be counted.

I said to myself, "Behold, I have obtained for myself great chakamah (wisdom) above all who were panayam (before) me in Yarawashalam. Yes, my lab (heart) has had great raah (see) of chakamah (wisdom) and daith (knowledge).
I applied my lab (heart) to yadai (know) chakamah (wisdom), and to yadai (know) madness and folly. I perceived that this also was a chasing after rawach (wind).
For in much chakamah (wisdom) is much kais (grief); and he who increases daith (knowledge) increases sorrow.
I said in my lab (heart), "yalak (come) now, I will test you with mirth: therefore raah (see) tawab (pleasure);" and behold, this also was vanity.
I said of laughter, "It is foolishness;" and of mirth, "What does it ishah (accomplish)?

I searched in my lab (heart) how to cheer my flesh with yayan (wine), my lab (heart) yet guiding me with chakamah (wisdom), and how to achaz (lay) hold of folly, until I might raah (see) what it was tawab (good) for the ban (sons) of men that they should do under shamayam (heaven) all the yawam (days) of their chay (lives).
I made myself great maishah (works). I built myself bayath (houses). I planted myself vineyards.
I made myself gardens and parks, and I planted itz (trees) in them of all kinds of fruit.
I made myself pools of mayam (water), to shaqah (water) from it the Yair Yair trees were reared.

I bought male ibad (servants) and female shapachah (servants), and had ban (servants) born in my bayath (house). I also had great maqanah (possessions) of herds and flocks, above all who were panayam (before) me in Yarawashalam;

I also gathered kasap (silver) and gold for myself, and the treasure of malak (kings) and of the provinces. I got myself male and female singers, and the delights of the ban (sons) of men—musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
So I was great, and increased more panayam (than) all who were before me in Yarawashalam. My chakamah (wisdom) also remained with me.

Whatever my iyan (eyes) desired, I didn't keep from them. I didn't withhold my lab (heart) from any joy, for my lab (heart) Shamach because of all my imal (labor), and this was my chalaq (portion) from all my imal (labor).

Then I looked at all the maishah (works) that my yad (hands) had worked, and at the imal (labor) that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after rawach (wind), and there was no profit under the shamash (sun).
I turned myself to raah (see) chakamah (wisdom), madness, and folly: for what can the malak (king's) successor do? Just that which has been done long ago.
Then I saw that chakamah (wisdom) excels folly, as far as awar (light) excels chashak (darkness).
The wise chakam (man's) iyan (eyes) are in his raash (head), and the Kasayal halak (walks) in darkness—and yet I perceived that one event qarah (happens) to them all.
Then I said in my lab (heart), "As it happens to the Kasayal, so will it qarah (happen) even to me; and why was I then more chakam (wise)?" Then I said in my lab (heart) that this also is vanity.

For of the chakam (wise) im (man), even as of the Kasayal, there is no memory for ever, since in the yawam (days) to bawaa (come) all will have been long forgotten. Indeed, the chakam (wise) mawath (man) must die just like the Kasayal!
So I hated chay (life), because the maishah (work) that is worked under the shamash (sun) was rai (grievous) to me; for all is vanity and a chasing after rawach (wind).
I hated all my imal (labor) in which I labored under the shamash (sun), because I must yanach (leave) it to the adam (man) who comes achar (after) me.

Who yadai (knows) whether he will be a chakam (wise) sakal (man) or a fool? Yet he will have shalat (rule) over all of my imal (labor) in which I have labored, and in which I have shown myself chakam (wise) under the shamash (sun). This also is vanity.
Therefore I began to cause my lab (heart) to despair concerning all the imal (labor) in which I had labored under the shamash (sun).

For there is a adam (man) whose imal (labor) is with chakamah (wisdom), with daith (knowledge), and with skillfulness; yet he shall nathan (leave) it for his chalaq (portion) to a adam (man) who has not labored for it. This also is vanity and a rab (great) rai (evil).
For what has a adam (man) of all his imal (labor), and of the striving of his lab (heart), in which he labors under the shamash (sun)?
For all his yawam (days) are sorrows, and his travail is kais (grief); yes, even in the layal (night) his lab (heart) takes no shakab (rest). This also is vanity.

There is nothing tawab (better) for a adam (man) than that he should akal (eat) and drink, and make his napash (soul) raah (see) tawab (good) in his imal (labor). This also I saw, that it is from the yad (hand) of Alahayam.
For who can akal (eat), or who can have enjoyment, more than I?

For to the adam (man) who pleases him, Alahayam gives chakamah (wisdom), daith (knowledge), and joy; but to the sinner he nathan (gives) travail, to asap (gather) and to heap up, that he may nathan (give) to him who pleases Alahayam. This also is vanity and a chasing after rawach (wind).
For everything there is a season, and a time for every Chapatz under shamayam (heaven):
a ith (time) to be yalad (born), and a ith (time) to mawath (die); a ith (time) to plant, and a ith (time) to pluck up that which is planted;
a ith (time) to harag (kill), and a ith (time) to heal; a ith (time) to break down, and a ith (time) to banah (build) up;
a ith (time) to weep, and a ith (time) to laugh; a ith (time) to mourn, and a ith (time) to dance;
a ith (time) to cast away aban (stones), and a ith (time) to gather aban (stones) together; a ith (time) to embrace, and a ith (time) to rachaq (refrain) from embracing;
a ith (time) to seek, and a ith (time) to abad (lose); a ith (time) to shamar (keep), and a ith (time) to cast away;
a ith (time) to tear, and a ith (time) to sew; a ith (time) to chashah (keep) silence, and a ith (time) to dabar (speak);
a ith (time) to ahab (love), and a ith (time) to shanaa (hate); a ith (time) for war, and a ith (time) for shalawam (peace).
What profit has he who ishah (works) in that in which he labors?
I have seen the burden which Alahayam has given to the ban (sons) of men to be afflicted with.

He has made everything Yapah in its ith (time). He has also nathan (set) eternity in their lab (hearts), yet so that adam (man) can't matzaa (find) out the maishah (work) that Alahayam has done from the raash (beginning) even to the end.
I yadai (know) that there is nothing tawab (better) for them than to Shamach, and to do tawab (good) as long as they chay (live).
Also that every adam (man) should akal (eat) and drink, and raah (see) tawab (good) in all his imal (labor), is the mathath (gift) of Alahayam.

I yadai (know) that whatever Alahayam does, it shall be iwalam (forever). Nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it; and Alahayam has done it, that men should yaraa (fear) panayam (before) him.
That which is has been long ago, and that which is to be has been long ago: and Alahayam seeks again that which is passed away.
Moreover I saw under the shamash (sun), in the place of justice, that rashai (wickedness) was there; and in the place of tzadaq (righteousness), that rashai (wickedness) was there.
I said in my lab (heart), "Alahayam will shapat (judge) the tzadayaq (righteous) and the rashai (wicked); for there is a ith (time) there for every Chapatz and for every maishah (work).
I said in my lab (heart), "As for the ban (sons) of men, Alahayam Barar them, so that they may raah (see) that they themselves are like animals.

For that which happens to the ban (sons) of men happens to animals. Even one thing happens to them. As the one dies, so the other dies. Yes, they have all one rawach (breath); and adam (man) has no advantage over the animals: for all is vanity.
All halak (go) to one place. All are from the ipar (dust), and all shawab (turn back / repent) to ipar (dust) again.
Who yadai (knows) the rawach (spirit) of ban (man), whether it goes upward, and the rawach (spirit) of the animal, whether it goes downward to the aratz (earth)?

Therefore I saw that there is nothing tawab (better), than that a adam (man) should Shamach in his maishah (works); for that is his chalaq (portion): for who can bawaa (bring) him to raah (see) what will be achar (after) him?

Then I returned and saw all the oppressions that are done under the shamash (sun): and behold, the tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the yad (side) of their oppressors there was kach (power); but they had no comforter.
Therefore I praised the mawath (dead) who have been long mawath (dead) more than the chay (living) who are yet chay (alive).
Yes, tawab (better) than them shanayam (both) is him who has not yet been, who has not seen the rai (evil) maishah (work) that is done under the shamash (sun).
Then I saw all the imal (labor) and achievement that is the envy of a ayash (man's) neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after rawach (wind).
The Kasayal folds his yad (hands) together and ruins himself.
tawab (better) is a kap (handful), with nachath (quietness), than two handfuls with imal (labor) and chasing after rawach (wind).
Then I returned and saw vanity under the shamash (sun).

There is one who is alone, and he has neither ban (son) nor ach (brother). There is no end to all of his imal (labor), neither are his iyan (eyes) satisfied with wealth. "For whom then, do I labor, and deprive my napash (soul) of enjoyment?" This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.
shanayam (two) are tawab (better) than one, because they have a tawab (good) reward for their imal (labor).
For if they napal (fall), the one will qawam (lift) up his fellow; but woe to him who is achad (alone) when he napal (falls), and doesn't have shanay (another) to qawam (lift) him up.
Again, if shanayam (two) shakab (lie) together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm yacham (alone)?
If a achad (man) prevails against one who is alone, shanayam (two) shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
tawab (better) is a Masakan and chakam (wise) youth than an zaqan (old) and Kasayal malak (king) who doesn't yadai (know) how to receive admonition any more.
For out of prison he came forth to be malak (king); yes, even in his malakawath (kingdom) he was yalad (born) poor.
I saw all the chay (living) who halak (walk) under the shamash (sun), that they were with the youth, the other, who succeeded him.
There was no end of all the im (people), even of all them over whom he was—yet those who Acharawan after shall not Shamach in him. Surely this also is vanity and a chasing after rawach (wind).

Guard your steps when you yalak (go) to alahayam (god's) bayath (house); for to draw qarawab (near) to listen is better than to nathan (give) the zabach (sacrifice) of Kasayal, for they don't yadai (know) that they do rai (evil).

Don't be rash with your pah (mouth), and don't let your lab (heart) be hasty to yatzaa (utter) anything panayam (before) Alahayam; for Alahayam is in shamayam (heaven), and you on aratz (earth). Therefore let your dabar (words) be Mait.
For as a chalawam (dream) bawaa (comes) with a multitude of cares, so a Kasayal speech with a multitude of dabar (words).
When you nadar (vow) a nadar (vow) to Alahayam, don't defer to shalam (pay) it; for he has no Chapatz in Kasayal. shalam (pay) that which you nadar (vow).
It is tawab (better) that you should not nadar (vow), than that you should nadar (vow) and not shalam (pay).

Don't allow your pah (mouth) to lead you into chataa (sin). Don't protest panayam (before) the malaak (messenger) that this was a mistake. Why should Alahayam be qatzap (angry) at your qawal (voice), and chabal (destroy) the maishah (work) of your yad (hands)?
For in the multitude of chalawam (dreams) there are vanities, as well as in many dabar (words): but you must yaraa (fear) Alahayam.

If you raah (see) the oppression of the poor, and the violent taking away of tzadaq (justice) and righteousness in a district, don't thamah (marvel) at the Chapatz: Gabah one official is eyed by a Gabah Gabah; and there are officials over them.
Moreover the profit of the aratz (earth) is for all. The malak (king) profits from the shadah (field).
He who ahab (loves) kasap (silver) shall not be satisfied with kasap (silver); nor he who ahab (loves) abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.
When tawab (goods) increase, those who akal (eat) them are increased; and what advantage is there to its owner, am (except) to feast on them with his iyan (eyes)?
The shanah (sleep) of a laboring ibad (man) is Mathawaq, whether he akal (eats) Mait or much; but the abundance of the Ishayar will not allow him to sleep.
There is a chalah (grievous) rai (evil) which I have seen under the shamash (sun): wealth kept by its owner to his rai (harm).
Those riches abad (perish) by misfortune, and if he has fathered a ban (son), there is nothing in his yad (hand).

As he came yatzaa (forth) from his am (mother's) womb, Irawam shall he yalak (go) again as he came, and shall nashaa (take) nothing for his imal (labor), which he may yalak (carry) away in his yad (hand).
This also is a chalah (grievous) rai (evil), that in all points as he came, so shall he yalak (go). And what profit does he have who imal (labors) for the rawach (wind)?
All his yawam (days) he also akal (eats) in chashak (darkness), he is frustrated, and has sickness and qatzap (wrath).

raah (see), that which I have seen to be tawab (good) and Yapah is for one to akal (eat) and to drink, and to raah (see) tawab (good) in all his imal (labor), in which he imal (labors) under the shamash (sun), all the yawam (days) of his chay (life) which Alahayam has given him; for this is his chalaq (portion).

Every adam (man) also to whom Alahayam has given riches and wealth, and has given him shalat (power) to akal (eat) of it, and to nashaa (take) his chalaq (portion), and to Shamach in his imal (labor) — this is the mathath (gift) of Alahayam.
For he shall not often reflect on the yawam (days) of his chay (life); because Alahayam occupies him with the joy of his lab (heart).
There is an rai (evil) which I have seen under the shamash (sun), and it is heavy on men:

a ayash (man) to whom Alahayam nathan (gives) riches, wealth, and honor, so that he Chasar nothing for his napash (soul) of all that he desires, yet Alahayam gives him no shalat (power) to akal (eat) of it, but an alien akal (eats) it. This is vanity, and it is an rai (evil) disease.

If a ayash (man) fathers a maah (hundred) children, and chayah (lives) many Shanah, so that the yawam (days) of his Shanah are many, but his napash (soul) is not filled with tawab (good), and moreover he has no qabawarah (burial); I amar (say), that a stillborn child is tawab (better) than he:
for it bawaa (comes) in vanity, and departs in chashak (darkness), and its sham (name) is covered with chashak (darkness).
Moreover it has not seen the shamash (sun) nor yadai (known) it. This has nachath (rest) rather zah (than) the other.
Yes, though he chayah (live) a alap (thousand) Shanah paim (twice) told, and yet fails to raah (see) tawab (good), don't all halak (go) to one place?
All the imal (labor) of adam (man) is for his pah (mouth), and yet the napash (appetite) is not filled.
For what advantage has the chakam (wise) more than the Kasayal? What has the Inay yadai (man), that knows how to halak (walk) before the chay (living)?
tawab (better) is the sight of the iyan (eyes) than the wandering of the napash (desire). This also is vanity and a chasing after rawach (wind).
Whatever has been, its qaraa (name) was given long ago; and it is yadai (known) what adam (man) is; neither can he contend with him who is mightier than he.
For there are many dabar (words) that rabah (create) vanity. What does that profit adam (man)?

For who yadai (knows) what is tawab (good) for adam (man) in chay (life), all the yawam (days) of his vain chay (life) which he ishah (spends) like a shadow? For who can nagad (tell) a adam (man) what will be achar (after) him under the shamash (sun)?
A good sham (name) is tawab (better) than tawab (fine) perfume; and the yawam (day) of mawath (death) better than the yawam (day) of one's yalad (birth).

It is tawab (better) to yalak (go) to the bayath (house) of mourning than to yalak (go) to the bayath (house) of feasting: for that is the end of all men, and the chay (living) should nathan (take) this to lab (heart).
kais (sorrow) is tawab (better) than laughter; for by the rai (sadness) of the panayam (face) the lab (heart) is made yatab (good).
The lab (heart) of the chakam (wise) is in the bayath (house) of mourning; but the lab (heart) of Kasayal is in the bayath (house) of mirth.
It is tawab (better) to hear the rebuke of the chakam (wise), than for a ayash (man) to hear the song of Kasayal.
For as the qawal (crackling) of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the Kasayal. This also is vanity.
Surely extortion makes the wise chakam (man) foolish; and a bribe abad (destroys) the lab (understanding).
tawab (better) is the acharayath (end) of a thing than its raashayath (beginning). The Arak in rawach (spirit) is tawab (better) than the Gabah in rawach (spirit).
Don't be hasty in your rawach (spirit) to be kais (angry), for kais (anger) nawach (rests) in the bosom of Kasayal.
Don't amar (say), "Why were the raashawan (former) yawam (days) tawab (better) than these?" For you do not shaal (ask) chakamah (wisely) about this.
chakamah (wisdom) is as tawab (good) as an nachalah (inheritance). Yes, it is more excellent for those who raah (see) the shamash (sun).
For chakamah (wisdom) is a defense, even as kasap (money) is a defense; but the excellency of daith (knowledge) is that chakamah (wisdom) preserves the chayah (life) of him who has it.
raah (see) the maishah (work) of Alahayam, for who can make that thaqan (straight), which he has made iwath (crooked)?

In the yawam (day) of tawab (prosperity) be tawab (joyful), and in the yawam (day) of rai (adversity) raah (see); yes, Alahayam has made the imah (one) side by side with the other, to the end that adam (man) should not matzaa (find) out anything achar (after) him.

All this have I seen in my yawam (days) of vanity: there is a tzadayaq (righteous) man who perishes in his tzadaq (righteousness), and there is a rashai (wicked) arak (man) who lives long in his evildoing.
Don't be overly tzadayaq (righteous), neither make yourself overly chakam (wise). Why should you shamam (destroy) yourself?
Don't be too rashai (wicked), neither be foolish. Why should you mawath (die) before your ith (time)?
It is tawab (good) that you should achaz (take) hold of this. Yes, also from that don't yanach (withdraw) your yad (hand); for he who yaraa (fears) Alahayam will yatzaa (come) forth from them all.
chakamah (wisdom) is a izaz (strength) to the chakam (wise) man more than ishar (ten) shalayat (rulers) who are in a Iyar.
Surely there is not a tzadayaq (righteous) adam (man) on aratz (earth), who does tawab (good) and doesn't chataa (sin).
Also don't nathan (take) lab (heed) to all dabar (words) that are spoken, lest you hear your ibad (servant) qalal (curse) you;
for often your own lab (heart) yadai (knows) that you yourself have likewise cursed others.
All this have I proved in chakamah (wisdom). I said, "I will be chakam (wise);" but it was Rachawaq from me.
That which is, is Rachawaq off and exceedingly Imaq. Who can matzaa (find) it out?

I turned around, and my lab (heart) sought to yadai (know) and to search out, and to seek chakamah (wisdom) and the scheme of things, and to yadai (know) that rashai (wickedness) is stupidity, and that foolishness is madness.

I matzaa (find) more Mar than mawath (death) the ashah (woman) whose lab (heart) is snares and traps, whose yad (hands) are chains. Whoever pleases Alahayam shall malat (escape) from her; but the sinner will be ensnared by her.
"raah (see), I have found this," amar (says) the Preacher, "one to another, to matzaa (find) out the scheme;
which my napash (soul) still seeks; but I have not found. One adam (man) among a alap (thousand) have I found; but I have not found a ashah (woman) among all those.
raah (see), this only have I found: that Alahayam made adam (man) yashar (upright); but they search for many schemes.

Who is like the chakam (wise) yadai (man)? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A adam (man's) chakamah (wisdom) makes his panayam (face) awar (shine), and the hardness of his panayam (face) is changed.
I say, "shamar (keep) the malak (king's) command!" because of the shabawaih (oath) to Alahayam.
Don't be hasty to yalak (go) out of his panayam (presence). Don't persist in an rai (evil) thing, for he does whatever pleases him,
for the malak (king's) dabar (word) is supreme. Who can amar (say) to him, "What are you doing?
Whoever shamar (keeps) the matzawah (commandment) shall not yadai (come) to rai (harm), and his wise lab (heart) will yadai (know) the ith (time) and procedure.
For there is a ith (time) and procedure for every Chapatz, although the rai (misery) of adam (man) is heavy on him.
For he doesn't yadai (know) that which will be; for who can nagad (tell) him how it will be?

There is no adam (man) who has shalayat (power) over the rawach (spirit) to contain the rawach (spirit); neither does he have shalatawan (power) over the yawam (day) of mawath (death). There is no discharge in war; neither shall rashai (wickedness) malat (deliver) those who practice it.

All this have I seen, and applied my lab (mind) to every maishah (work) that is done under the shamash (sun). There is a ith (time) in which one adam (man) has shalat (power) over another to his rai (hurt).
So I saw the rashai (wicked) buried. bawaa (indeed) they came also from maqawam (holiness). They went and were forgotten in the Iyar where they did this. This also is vanity.
Because sentence against an rai (evil) maishah (work) is not executed speedily, therefore the lab (heart) of the ban (sons) of men is fully malaa (set) in them to do rai (evil).

Though a sinner ishah (commits) crimes a maah (hundred) times, and lives long, yet surely I yadai (know) that it will be tawab (better) with those who yaraa (fear) Alahayam, who are reverent panayam (before) him.
But it shall not be tawab (well) with the rashai (wicked), neither shall he lengthen yawam (days) like a shadow; panayam (because) he doesn't yaraa (fear) Alahayam.

There is a vanity which is done on the aratz (earth), that there are tzadayaq (righteous) men to whom it nagai (happens) according to the maishah (work) of the rashai (wicked). Again, there are rashai (wicked) men to whom it nagai (happens) according to the maishah (work) of the tzadayaq (righteous). I said that this also is vanity.

Then I commended mirth, because a adam (man) has no tawab (better) thing under the shamash (sun), than to akal (eat), and to drink, and to be Shamach: for that will accompany him in his imal (labor) all the yawam (days) of his chay (life) which Alahayam has given him under the shamash (sun).

When I applied my lab (heart) to yadai (know) chakamah (wisdom), and to raah (see) the business that is done on the aratz (earth) (for also there is that neither yawam (day) nor layal (night) raah (see) shanah (sleep) with his iyan (eyes)),

then I saw all the maishah (work) of Alahayam, that adam (man) can't matzaa (find) out the maishah (work) that is done under the shamash (sun), because however much a adam (man) imal (labors) to seek it out, yet he won't matzaa (find) it. Yes even though a chakam (wise) man amar (thinks) he can yadai (comprehend) it, he won't be yakal (able) to matzaa (find) it.

For all this I laid to my lab (heart), even to explore all this: that the tzadayaq (righteous), and the chakam (wise), and their ibad (works), are in the yad (hand) of Alahayam; whether it is ahabah (love) or hatred, adam (man) doesn't yadai (know) it; all is panayam (before) them.

All things come achad (alike) to all. There is one event to the tzadayaq (righteous) and to the rashai (wicked); to the tawab (good), to the tahawar (clean), to the tamaa (unclean), to him who zabach (sacrifices), and to him who doesn't zabach (sacrifice). As is the tawab (good), so is the sinner; he who shabai (takes) an oath, as he who yaraa (fears) an shabawaih (oath).

This is an rai (evil) in all that is done under the shamash (sun), that there is one event to all: yes also, the lab (heart) of the ban (sons) of men is malaa (full) of rai (evil), and madness is in their labab (heart) while they chay (live), and achar (after) that they go to the mawath (dead).
For to him who is joined with all the chay (living) there is hope; for a chay (living) dog is tawab (better) than a mawath (dead) aray (lion).
For the chay (living) yadai (know) that they will mawath (die), but the mawath (dead) don't yadai (know) anything, neither do they have any more a reward; for their zakar (memory) is forgotten.
Also their ahabah (love), their hatred, and their envy has perished long ago; neither have they any more a chalaq (portion) iwalam (forever) in anything that is done under the shamash (sun).
Go your yalak (way) — akal (eat) your lacham (bread) with joy, and drink your yayan (wine) with a tawab (merry) lab (heart); for Alahayam has already accepted your maishah (works).
Let your bagad (garments) be ith (always) Laban, and don't let your raash (head) lack shaman (oil).

chay (live) raah (see) with the ashah (wife) whom you ahab (love) all the yawam (days) of your chay (life) of vanity, which he has given you under the shamash (sun), all your yawam (days) of vanity: for that is your chalaq (portion) in chay (life), and in your imal (labor) in which you labor under the shamash (sun).

Whatever your yad (hand) matzaa (finds) to do, do it with your might; for there is no maishah (work), nor device, nor daith (knowledge), nor chakamah (wisdom), in shaawal (sheol), where you are going.

I returned, and saw under the shamash (sun), that the race is not to the qal (swift), nor the battle to the gabawar (strong), neither yet lacham (bread) to the chakam (wise), nor yet riches to men of bayan (understanding), nor yet favor to men of yadai (skill); but ith (time) and chance qarah (happen) to them all.

For adam (man) also doesn't yadai (know) his ith (time). As the fish that are taken in an rai (evil) net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare, even so are the ban (sons) of men snared in an rai (evil) ith (time), when it napal (falls) suddenly on them.
I have also seen chakamah (wisdom) under the shamash (sun) in this way, and it seemed gadawal (great) to me.
There was a qatan (little) Iyar, and Mait men within it; and a gadawal (great) malak (king) came against it, besieged it, and built gadawal (great) bulwarks against it.
Now a Masakan chakam (wise) ayash (man) was found in it, and he by his wisdom delivered the Iyar; yet no adam (man) zakar (remembered) that same Masakan adam (man).
Then I said, "chakamah (wisdom) is tawab (better) than gabawarah (strength)." Nevertheless the Masakan man's chakamah (wisdom) is despised, and his dabar (words) are not heard.
The dabar (words) of the chakam (wise) heard in nachath (quiet) are better than the cry of him who mashal (rules) among Kasayal.
chakamah (wisdom) is tawab (better) than weapons of war; but one sinner abad (destroys) much tawab (good).
mawath (dead) flies cause the shaman (oil) of the perfumer to send forth an evil odor; so does a Mait folly Yaqar chakamah (wisdom) and honor.
A wise chakam (man's) lab (heart) is at his right yamayan (hand), but a Kasayal lab (heart) at his shamaawal (left).
Yes also, when the fool halak (walks) by the darak (way), his lab (understanding) Chasar him, and he amar (says) to everyone that he is a fool.
If the rawach (spirit) of the ruler ilah (rises) up against you, don't yanach (leave) your place; for gentleness yanach (lays) gadawal (great) offenses to rest.
There is an rai (evil) which I have seen under the shamash (sun), the sort of error which yatzaa (proceeds) from the shalayat (ruler).
Folly is nathan (set) in rab (great) dignity, and the Ishayar yashab (sit) in a low place.
I have seen ibad (servants) on horses, and shar (princes) walking like ibad (servants) on the aratz (earth).
He who digs a gawamatz (pit) may napal (fall) into it; and whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
Whoever carves out aban (stones) may be injured by them. Whoever splits itz (wood) may be endangered thereby.
If the axe is blunt, and one doesn't sharpen the panayam (edge), then he must use more chayal (strength); but skill brings success.
If the snake bites before it is charmed, then is there no profit for the charmer's lashawan (tongue).
The dabar (words) of a wise chakam (man's) pah (mouth) are gracious; but a Kasayal is swallowed by his own shapah (lips).
The thachalah (beginning) of the dabar (words) of his pah (mouth) is foolishness; and the acharayath (end) of his pah (talk) is rai (mischievous) madness.
A fool also multiplies dabar (words). adam (man) doesn't yadai (know) what will be; and that which will be achar (after) him, who can nagad (tell) him?
The imal (labor) of Kasayal wearies every one of them; for he doesn't yadai (know) how to yalak (go) to the Iyar.
Woe to you, aratz (land), when your malak (king) is a nair (child), and your shar (princes) akal (eat) in the baqar (morning)!
Happy are you, aratz (land), when your malak (king) is the ban (son) of nobles, and your shar (princes) akal (eat) in due ith (season), for gabawarah (strength), and not for drunkenness!
By slothfulness the roof sinks in; and through idleness of the yad (hands) the bayath (house) leaks.
A feast is made for laughter, and yayan (wine) Shamach the life glad; and kasap (money) is the answer for all things.

Don't qalal (curse) the malak (king), no, not in your madai (thoughts); and don't qalal (curse) the Ishayar in your bedroom: for a bird of the sky may yalak (carry) your qawal (voice), and that which has wings may nagad (tell) the dabar (matter).
shalach (cast) your lacham (bread) on the mayam (waters); for you shall matzaa (find) it after many yawam (days).
nathan (give) a chalaq (portion) to shabai (seven), yes, even to shamanah (eight); for you don't yadai (know) what rai (evil) will be on the aratz (earth).

If the clouds are malaa (full) of rain, they empty themselves on the aratz (earth); and if a itz (tree) napal (falls) toward the south, or toward the tzapawan (north), in the place where the itz (tree) napal (falls), there shall it be.
He who shamar (observes) the rawach (wind) won't zarai (sow); and he who raah (see) the clouds won't reap.

As you don't yadai (know) what is the darak (way) of the rawach (wind), nor how the itzam (bones) grow in the womb of her who is with Malaa; even so you don't yadai (know) the maishah (work) of Alahayam who does all.

In the baqar (morning) zarai (sow) your zarai (seed), and in the evening don't yanach (withhold) your yad (hand); for you don't yadai (know) which will kashar (prosper), whether this or that, or whether they shanayam (both) will be equally tawab (good).
Truly the awar (light) is Mathawaq, and a tawab (pleasant) thing it is for the iyan (eyes) to raah (see) the shamash (sun).

Yes, if a adam (man) chayah (lives) many Shanah, let him Shamach in them all; but let him zakar (remember) the yawam (days) of chashak (darkness), for they shall be many. All that bawaa (comes) is vanity.

Shamach, young bachawar (man), in your youth, and let your lab (heart) tawab (cheer) you in the yawam (days) of your youth, and halak (walk) in the darak (ways) of your lab (heart), and in the sight of your maraah (eyes); but yadai (know) that for all these things Alahayam will bawaa (bring) you into mashapat (judgment).
Therefore sawar (remove) kais (sorrow) from your lab (heart), and ibar (put) away rai (evil) from your flesh; for youth and the dawn of habal (life) are vanity.

zakar (remember) also your Creator in the yawam (days) of your youth, before the rai (evil) yawam (days) bawaa (come), and the Shanah nagai (draw) near, when you will amar (say), "I have no Chapatz in them;
Before the shamash (sun), the awar (light), the yarach (moon), and the kawakab (stars) are darkened, and the clouds shawab (turn back / repent) achar (after) the rain;

in the yawam (day) when the keepers of the bayath (house) shall tremble, and the chayal (strong) men shall iwath (bow) themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who raah (see) out of the windows are darkened,

and the doors shall be shut in the street; when the qawal (sound) of the grinding is Shapal, and one shall qawam (rise) up at the qawal (voice) of a bird, and all the bath (daughters) of music shall be brought low;

yes, they shall be yaraa (afraid) of Gabah, and terrors will be in the darak (way); and the almond tree shall blossom, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall parar (fail); because adam (man) goes to his iwalam (forever) bayath (home), and the mourners sabab (go) about the streets:
laa (before) the kasap (silver) cord is severed, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is shabar (broken) at the spring, or the galagal (wheel) broken at the bawar (cistern),
and the ipar (dust) shawab (turn back / repent) to the aratz (earth) as it was, and the rawach (spirit) shawab (turn back / repent) to Alahayam who gave it.
"Vanity of vanities," amar (says) the Preacher. "All is vanity!
Further, because the Preacher was chakam (wise), he still taught the im (people) daith (knowledge). Yes, he pondered, sought out, and thaqan (set) in order many proverbs.
The Preacher sought to matzaa (find) out Chapatz dabar (words), and that which was written blamelessly, dabar (words) of truth.
The dabar (words) of the chakam (wise) are like goads; and like nails well fastened are words from the bail (masters) of asapah (assemblies), which are given from one raih (shepherd).
Furthermore, my ban (son), be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
This is the end of the dabar (matter). All has been heard. yaraa (fear) Alahayam, and shamar (keep) his matzawah (commandments); for this is the whole duty of adam (man).
For Alahayam will bawaa (bring) every maishah (work) into mashapat (judgment), with every hidden thing, whether it is tawab (good), or whether it is rai (evil).
The Song of songs, which is Shalamah. Beloved
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his pah (mouth); for your dawad (love) is tawab (better) than yayan (wine).
Your shaman (oils) have a pleasing fragrance. Your sham (name) is shaman (oil) poured forth, therefore the virgins ahab (love) you.

Take me achar (away) with you. Let us hurry. The malak (king) has brought me into his rooms. Friends We will be glad and Shamach in you. We will praise your dawad (love) more than yayan (wine)! Beloved They are mayashar (right) to ahab (love) you.
I am Shachar, but lovely, you bath (daughters) of Yarawashalam, like Qadar ahal (tents), like Shalamah curtains.

Don't raah (see) Shacharacharath me because I am dark, because the shamash (sun) has scorched me. My am (mother's) ban (sons) were charar (angry) with me. They made me keeper of the vineyards. I haven't kept my own vineyard.

nagad (tell) me, you whom my napash (soul) ahab (loves), where you graze your flock, where you rabatz (rest) them at tzahar (noon); For why should I be as idar (one) who is veiled beside the flocks of your companions? Lover
If you don't yadai (know), most Yapah among women, follow the tracks of the sheep. Graze your young goats beside the raih (shepherds)' mashakan (tents).
I have compared you, my raiyah (love), to a steed in Paraih chariots.
Your Lachay are beautiful with earrings, your neck with strings of jewels.
We will ishah (make) you earrings of gold, with studs of kasap (silver). Beloved
While the malak (king) sat at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance.
My dawad (beloved) is to me a sachet of myrrh, that lies between my breasts.
My dawad (beloved) is to me a cluster of henna blossoms from the vineyards of Iyanagaday Gedi. Lover
Behold, you are Yapah, my raiyah (love). Behold, you are Yapah. Your iyan (eyes) are doves. Beloved
Behold, you are Yapah, my dawad (beloved), yes, Naiyam; and our couch is Rainan. Lover
The beams of our bayath (house) are cedars. Our rafters are firs.
I am a rose of Sharawan, a lily of the valleys. Lover
As a lily among thorns, so is my raiyah (love) among the bath (daughters). Beloved
As the apple tree among the itz (trees) of the Yair, so is my dawad (beloved) among the ban (sons). I sat down under his shadow with great delight, his fruit was Mathawaq to my chak (taste).
He brought me to the banquet hall. His banner over me is ahabah (love).
Strengthen me with raisins, refresh me with apples; For I am faint with ahabah (love).
His left shamaawal (hand) is under my raash (head). His right yamayan (hand) embraces me.
I shabai (adjure) you, bath (daughters) of Yarawashalam, by the tzabay (roes), or by the hinds of the shadah (field), that you not stir up, nor awaken ahabah (love), until it so desires.
The qawal (voice) of my dawad (beloved)! Behold, he bawaa (comes), leaping on the har (mountains), skipping on the Gabaih.
My dawad (beloved) is like a tzabay (roe) or a young hart. Behold, he imad (stands) achar (behind) our wall! He looks in at the windows. He glances through the lattice.
My dawad (beloved) spoke, and said to me, "qawam (rise) up, my raiyah (love), my Yapah one, and yalak (come) away.
For, behold, the winter is past. The rain is over and gone.
The flowers raah (see) on the aratz (earth). The ith (time) of the singing has nagai (come), and the qawal (voice) of the turtledove is heard in our aratz (land).
The fig tree ripens her green figs. The vines are in blossom. They nathan (give) forth their fragrance. qawam (arise), my raiyah (love), my Yapah one, and yalak (come) away." Lover

My dove in the clefts of the salai (rock), In the hiding places of the mountainside, Let me raah (see) your maraah (face). Let me hear your qawal (voice); for your qawal (voice) is Irab, and your maraah (face) is lovely.
achaz (catch) for us the foxes, the qatan (little) foxes that chabal (spoil) the vineyards; for our vineyards are in blossom. Beloved
My dawad (beloved) is mine, and I am his. He browses among the lilies.
Until the yawam (day) is cool, and the shadows flee away, sabab (turn), my dawad (beloved), and be like a tzabay (roe) or a young hart on the har (mountains) of Bether.
By layal (night) on my bed, I sought him whom my napash (soul) ahab (loves). I sought him, but I didn't matzaa (find) him.
I will qawam (get) up now, and sabab (go) about the Iyar; in the streets and in the squares I will seek him whom my napash (soul) ahab (loves). I sought him, but I didn't matzaa (find) him.
The watchmen who sabab (go) about the Iyar found me; "Have you seen him whom my napash (soul) ahab (loves)?

I had Mait passed from them, when I found him whom my napash (soul) ahab (loves). I held him, and would not let him rapah (go), until I had brought him into my am (mother's) bayath (house), into the room of her who conceived me.
I shabai (adjure) you, bath (daughters) of Yarawashalam, by the tzabay (roes), or by the hinds of the shadah (field), that you not stir up, nor awaken ahabah (love), until it so desires.
Who is this who ilah (comes) up from the madabar (wilderness) like pillars of ishan (smoke), perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all spices of the merchant?
Behold, it is Shalamah carriage! shashayam (sixty) gabawar (mighty) men are around it, of the gabawar (mighty) men of Yasharaal (Israel).
They all achaz (handle) the charab (sword), and are expert in war. Every ayash (man) has his charab (sword) on his thigh, because of pachad (fear) in the layal (night).
malak (king) Shalamah made himself a carriage of the itz (wood) of Labanawan.
He made its pillars of kasap (silver), its bottom of gold, its seat of purple, its midst being paved with ahabah (love), from the bath (daughters) of Yarawashalam.

yatzaa (go) forth, you bath (daughters) of Tzayawan, and raah (see) malak (king) Shalamah, with the itarah (crown) with which his am (mother) has crowned him, in the yawam (day) of his weddings, in the yawam (day) of the gladness of his lab (heart). Lover
Behold, you are Yapah, my raiyah (love). Behold, you are Yapah. Your iyan (eyes) are doves behind your tzamah (veil). Your hair is as a flock of goats, that descend from har (mount) Galaid.
Your teeth are like a newly shorn flock, which have ilah (come) up from the washing, where every one of them has Thaam. None is Shakawal among them.
Your shapah (lips) are like scarlet thread. Your mouth is lovely. Your raqah (temples) are like a piece of a pomegranate behind your tzamah (veil).
Your neck is like Dawad magadal (tower) built for an armory, whereon a alap (thousand) magan (shields) hang, all the shalat (shields) of the gabawar (mighty) men.
Your shanayam (two) breasts are like shanayam (two) fawns that are twins of a roe, which raih (feed) among the lilies.
Until the yawam (day) is cool, and the shadows flee away, I will yalak (go) to the har (mountain) of myrrh, to the Gabaih of frankincense.
You are all Yapah, my raiyah (love). There is no spot in you.

bawaa (come) with me from Labanawan, my kalah (bride), with me from Labanawan. Look from the raash (top) of Amanah, from the raash (top) of Shanayar and Charamawan, from the aray (lions)' dens, from the harar (mountains) of the leopards.
You have ravished my labab (heart), my achawath (sister), my kalah (bride). You have ravished my labab (heart) with one of your iyan (eyes), with one chain of your neck.
How beautiful is your dawad (love), my achawath (sister), my kalah (bride)! How much tawab (better) is your dawad (love) than yayan (wine)! The fragrance of your perfumes than all kinds of spices!
Your shapah (lips), my kalah (bride), drip like the honeycomb. Honey and milk are under your lashawan (tongue). The rayach (smell) of your garments is like the rayach (smell) of Labanawan.
A locked up Gan is my achawath (sister), my kalah (bride); a locked up spring, a sealed fountain.
Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates, with precious fruits: henna with spikenard plants,
spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with every kind of incense itz (tree); myrrh and aloes, with all the best spices,
a fountain of Gan, a baar (well) of chay (living) mayam (waters), nazal (flowing) streams from Labanawan. Beloved

Awake, north tzapawan (wind); and bawaa (come), you thayaman (south)! Blow on my Gan, that its spices may nazal (flow) out. Let my dawad (beloved) bawaa (come) into his Gan, and taste his precious fruits.

I have bawaa (come) into my Gan, my achawath (sister), my kalah (bride). I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my Yair Yair my honey; I have drunk my yayan (wine) with my milk. Friends akal (eat), rai (friends)! Drink, yes, Shakar abundantly, dawad (beloved). Beloved

I was yashan (asleep), but my lab (heart) was awake. It is the qawal (voice) of my dawad (beloved) who knocks: "pathach (open) to me, my achawath (sister), my raiyah (love), my dove, my tham (undefiled); for my raash (head) is filled with dew, and my hair with the dampness of the layal (night).
I have taken off my robe. Indeed, must I Labash it on? I have washed my feet. Indeed, must I soil them?
My dawad (beloved) thrust his yad (hand) in through the latch opening. My maih (heart) pounded for him.
I rose up to pathach (open) for my dawad (beloved). My yad (hands) dripped with myrrh, my fingers with liquid myrrh, on the handles of the lock.

I opened to my dawad (beloved); but my dawad (beloved) left; and had gone away. My napash (heart) went out when he spoke. I looked for him, but I didn't matzaa (find) him. I called him, but he didn't answer.
The watchmen who sabab (go) about the Iyar found me. They beat me. They bruised me. The keepers of the walls took my cloak nashaa (away) from me.
I shabai (adjure) you, bath (daughters) of Yarawashalam, If you matzaa (find) my dawad (beloved), that you nagad (tell) him that I am faint with ahabah (love). Friends
How is your dawad (beloved) better than another dawad (beloved), you Yapah among women? How is your dawad (beloved) better than another dawad (beloved), that you do so shabai (adjure) us? Beloved
My dawad (beloved) is Tzach and Adam. The best among rababah (ten) thousand.
His raash (head) is like the purest gold. His hair is bushy, Shachar as a raven.
His iyan (eyes) are like doves beside the mayam (water) apayaq (brooks), washed with milk, mounted like jewels.
His Lachay are like a bed of spices with towers of perfumes. His shapah (lips) are like lilies, natap (dropping) liquid myrrh.
His yad (hands) are like rings of gold malaa (set) with beryl. His body is like ivory ishath (work) overlaid with sapphires.
His legs are like pillars of Shash yasad (set) on sockets of fine gold. His appearance is like Labanawan, excellent as the cedars.
His chak (mouth) is sweetness; yes, he is altogether lovely. This is my dawad (beloved), and this is my rai (friend), bath (daughters) of Yarawashalam.
Where has your dawad (beloved) gone, you Yapah among women? Where has your dawad (beloved) turned, that we may seek him with you? Beloved
